cues.text: A Life Recorded Long After the Fact
David, known in Welsh as Dewi Sant, is traditionally said to have been born in the late fifth or early sixth century.
He was reportedly born near Menevia in southwestern Wales, the son of a local ruler named Sant or Sandde and a woman remembered as St. Non.
Almost every detail of this account, however, comes from a Life written by the Welsh cleric Rhygyfarch roughly five hundred years after David's death.
Later writers, including Geoffrey of Monmouth, considerably elaborated it.
This gap is wide enough that these particulars belong to long-standing tradition rather than contemporary record, and should be received accordingly.
An Ascetic Rule
Later tradition credits David with founding a dozen monasteries across Wales and beyond, including a major monastery at Menevia in Pembrokeshire, later known as St. David's.
The rule attributed to him was famously severe: the monks were said to pull their own ploughs rather than use draught animals and to drink only water.
They reportedly ate plain bread with salt and herbs and devoted their evenings to prayer, reading, and manual work.
Visitors and later chroniclers alike remembered this community less for comfort than for the intensity of its discipline.
A Voice at the Synods
David's later prominence in Welsh tradition rests chiefly on accounts of his role at the Synod of Brevi, held at what is now Llandewi Brefi in Cardiganshire, and at a second synod.

These accounts, like the details of his early life, derive largely from much later sources, so the extent of his historical role and the circumstances of his recognition as a leading bishop remain uncertain.
However, later tradition attached the title of archbishop to him based on devotional memory rather than a documented office of his own time.
Last Words to His Monks
As his own death approached, tradition holds that David gave his monks a final exhortation notable for its plainness rather than grand theological flourish.
He urged them simply to remain joyful, keep their faith and creed, and continue doing the small, ordinary things they had seen him do and heard him teach.
Whatever the precise wording preserved across so many centuries of retelling, the sentiment fits a saint remembered above all for demanding little except constancy.
Death and a Late Canonization

The earliest surviving reference to David, a tenth-century manuscript of the Annales Cambriae, places his death in the year 601, a date modern scholarship generally treats as more reliable than the earlier year of 544 that some later biographers preferred.

He was buried at his own monastery, where the cathedral that grew up around his shrine drew pilgrims throughout the Middle Ages; two pilgrimages to St. David's were popularly reckoned equal in merit to one to Rome.
Formal canonization came remarkably late, in 1120, when Pope Callistus II confirmed a devotion that had already flourished, by then, for over five hundred years.
Legacy
More than fifty churches across South Wales bore David's name before the Reformation.
The leek Welsh soldiers are said to have worn into battle at his advice, to distinguish themselves from their enemies, remains a national emblem.
It is worn every March 1 in his honor.
We find in David a model easy to overlook precisely because it asks for so little drama: no dramatic conversion, no martyrdom.
Only a rule kept faithfully, a synod addressed plainly, and a people who, fifteen centuries later, still call him simply Dewi Sant, their own.
